## Verdict
- Answer: Since 2023 the field's center of gravity moved from qubit-count milestones to error correction: below-threshold surface-code memory (2024), logical-qubit demonstrations on several platforms, and early fault-tolerance roadmaps. Practical advantage on useful problems is still unproven.
- Decision: Treat quantum as a staged, monitor-and-pilot investment (post-quantum cryptography migration now; algorithm and hardware pilots only where the use case is well-defined). Do not budget for near-term production advantage.
- Confidence: medium - findings come from memory of widely reported papers, not a live bibliometric query; no counts were measured.
- What would change it: A verified, independently reproduced advantage on a commercially relevant task, or a failed scaling of logical error suppression.

## What the data shows
No Prism calls were run, so no measured counts exist. All figures below come from memory and are labelled (est.) or tied to a reference. My knowledge ends June 2026, and I have no verified coverage of the last ~4 months before today (2026-10-23).

Key developments:
- **Below-threshold error correction.** Google reported a surface-code memory with distance 3, 5 and 7 on a 105-qubit Willow chip, with logical error suppressed by about 2× (est.) per distance step [r1]. An earlier 2023 paper showed a distance-5 code was marginally better than distance-3 [r2].
- **Logical qubits on neutral atoms.** Harvard/QuEra reported programmable logical-qubit processors with up to 48 logical qubits (est.) [r3].
- **Trapped ions.** Quantinuum and Microsoft reported logical-qubit experiments with 4 logical qubits (est.) and sizable logical-versus-physical error improvements [r4].
- **Efficient codes.** IBM proposed qLDPC "gross code" memory, claiming roughly 10× (est.) fewer physical qubits than surface codes [r5].
- **Resource estimates.** Gidney (2025) estimated RSA-2048 could be factored with under 1 million noisy qubits (est.) in about a week (est.), down from ~20 million (est.) in 2019 [r6].
- **Quantum advantage claims.** Random circuit sampling continued (Willow, 2024) [r1]; the 2023 IBM "utility" experiment on 127 qubits (est.) was soon matched by classical tensor-network simulation [r7]. This shows how classical rebuttals keep pace with claims.
- **Framing shift.** From "NISQ advantage" to "logical qubits, fault tolerance, resource estimates, and classical-simulation checks".
- **Policy/standards.** NIST finalized the first post-quantum standards in 2024 (FIPS 203/204/205) [r8].

## Trend
Illustrative, from memory: largest reported logical-qubit counts in published experiments.

```prism-chart

```

Quantified change: roughly 48× (est.) between 2023 and 2024 in this recalled metric, with high uncertainty about definitions, since the experiments' logical qubits differ in quality and are not comparable.

## Comparison
Baseline: RSA-2048 factoring physical-qubit estimate, 2019 versus 2025, same task, noisy-qubit assumptions.

| Estimate | Physical qubits | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Gidney & Ekerå 2019 | ~20,000,000 (est.) | [r9] |
| Gidney 2025 | <1,000,000 (est.) | [r6] |
| Delta | ~20× fewer (est.) | derived from above |

The comparison tracks algorithmic and code improvements, not hardware progress.

## Evidence
| Ref | Year | Venue | Tier | Claim supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [r1] | 2024/25 | Nature, Google Quantum AI | peer-reviewed | Below-threshold surface-code scaling |
| [r2] | 2023 | Nature | peer-reviewed | Distance-5 vs distance-3 comparison |
| [r3] | 2023 | Nature, Bluvstein et al. | peer-reviewed | Logical neutral-atom processors |
| [r4] | 2024 | Quantinuum/Microsoft preprint | preprint | Ion-trap logical qubits |
| [r5] | 2024 | Nature, IBM | peer-reviewed | qLDPC gross code |
| [r6] | 2025 | arXiv, Gidney | preprint | <1M qubit RSA-2048 |
| [r7] | 2023 | Nature (Kim et al.) and arXiv rebuttals | mixed | Utility claim and classical simulation response |
| [r8] | 2024 | NIST | standard | PQC standards |

No verbatim quotes are given, since I cannot verify exact wording from memory. Identifiers (DOIs) are not recalled reliably, so I leave them out rather than invent them. Citation counts and orientation (supportive vs critical) for each work are not measured here.

## Method and limits
- Windows: 2023-01-01 to roughly mid-2026 (my knowledge cutoff June 2026); gap to today (2026-10-23) is about 4 months unseen. The 2025 plateau in the chart reflects my recall, not evidence of stagnation.
- Lanes: research and standards only. News trend, citations, orientation shares, DOIs and under-covered topics could not be measured; the follow-ups above would measure them.
- Coverage and censoring: selected well-known results, biased toward high-profile Western labs and Nature-class venues; Chinese groups (e.g., Zuchongzhi, photonic Jiuzhang) are underrepresented here.
- Match mode: none; no corpus was queried.
- Counts are recalled approximations, not tallies. The plateau, "framing shift" and decision advice are my interpretation. The 1 → 48 figure compares non-equivalent experiments.

- [r2] Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit. Nature, 2023. doi not recalled.
- [r3] Logical quantum processor based on reconfigurable atom arrays. Nature, 2023/24. doi not recalled.

- [r7] Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance. Nature, 2023, plus classical simulation preprints.

## Verdict
- Answer: Quantum computing research output has risen about 18% a year since 2017 [c1], and news volume has risen faster. The most-cited new work is about utility before fault tolerance, photonic platforms, benchmarking and surveys [c1]. Framing is broadly unchanged [c1].
- Decision: This supports treating the field as fast-growing and active. It does not support judging which hardware approach is winning or when useful machines will arrive.
- Confidence: medium - one radar call covers volume, top-cited papers and framing. Titles and orientation labels are automated, and no call tested claims or performance.
- What would change it: Evidence calls on specific claims, such as utility or error correction, or a different keyword scope.

## What the data shows
**Research volume.** Papers matching "quantum computing" rose from 11,103 in 2017 to 41,759 in 2025, the peak year. That is a CAGR of 18.0% [c1]. The late third of the window totals 89,940 papers against 37,569 in the early third, a ratio of 2.39 [c1].

**News volume.** Monthly articles rose from 74 in January 2019 to 899 in May 2026, with a peak of 1,246 in April 2026. That is a CAGR of 40.6% [c1]. The late third totals 17,541 against 2,660 in the early third, a ratio of 6.59 [c1].

**New work since 2023.** The list below is the most-cited typed papers, filtered by title phrase [c1]. Citation counts are as reported in that call.

| Year | Title | Citations | Orientation | DOI |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance (Nature) | 956 [c1] | breakthrough | 10.1038/s41586-023-06096-3 |
| 2023 | A Survey of Important Issues in Quantum Computing and Communications | 217 [c1] | problem_identifying | 10.1109/comst.2023.3254481 |
| 2023 | Quantum Computing for Healthcare: A Review | 195 [c1] | breakthrough | 10.3390/fi15030094 |
| 2024 | A versatile single-photon-based quantum computing platform | 190 [c1] | breakthrough | 10.1038/s41566-024-01403-4 |
| 2024 | Quantum computing with Qiskit | 170 [c1] | descriptive | 10.48550/arxiv.2405.08810 |
| 2024 | Quantum Computing for High-Energy Physics | 160 [c1] | problem_identifying | 10.1103/prxquantum.5.037001 |
| 2024 | Distributed quantum computing: A survey | 156 [c1] | problem_identifying | 10.1016/j.comnet.2024.110672 |
| 2023 | MQT Bench | 145 [c1] | breakthrough | 10.22331/q-2023-07-20-1062 |
| 2025 | A manufacturable platform for photonic quantum computing (Nature) | 131 [c1] | breakthrough | 10.1038/s41586-025-08820-7 |
| 2023 | Application-Oriented Performance Benchmarks | 127 [c1] | breakthrough | 10.1109/tqe.2023.3253761 |

**Framing shift.** The cautionary share was 11.0% of 39,406 recent papers, against 8.9% of 51,192 earlier papers. The change is +2.1 percentage points, which the tool reads as "broadly unchanged" [c1]. Orientation labels the paper's own framing, not the truth [c1].

**Under-covered topics.** The tool returned zero news ledes for every research topic label, for example 93,160 papers on Algorithms and Architecture [c1]. The tool states that 0 means the taxonomy string never appears, not that the subject is uncovered. **I cannot measure under-coverage from this call.**

## Trend

## Comparison
Baseline: the early third of each series, in the same units as the late third [c1].

|---|---|---|---|---|

| News articles | 2,660 [c1] | 17,541 [c1] | 6.59 [c1] | 40.6% [c1] |

News grew about 2.8 times faster than papers on the ratio scale (6.59 / 2.39). The windows differ: papers run 2017–2025 and news runs 2019–May 2026. The comparison is therefore indicative, not like for like.

## Evidence
Only one source was available, the Prism radar [c1]. It lists Nature (2023) on utility before fault tolerance [r1] and Nature (2025) on a manufacturable photonic platform [r2]. No verbatim quotes were returned. The evidence tier is bibliographic metadata; I did not read the papers.

## Method and limits
- **Windows.** Papers run 2017–2025; the gap to today (2026-10-23) is at least 10 months. News runs 2019-01-01 to 2026-05-01, a gap of about 5.7 months.
- **Lane and coverage.** One research-plus-news radar call. Tables passed row-floor checks, which prove reachability, not ingest completeness [c1].

## Method and limits

The research trend window is 2017–2025 [c1]; the news window is 2019-01-01 through 2026-05-01 [c1], leaving a five-month gap to today (2026-10-23) [c1]. Radar’s selected-work window starts in 2023 [c1]. Its coverage metadata says the indexed tables passed index partition-read and historical-row-floor checks, but explicitly does not prove ingest completeness [c1]. The work list is selected by citation ranking and title phrase match [c1]. The tool gives aggregates and endpoints, not the underlying annual research series, article-level news evidence, or a deduplicated census. Counts and citation totals are database indicators; “momentum,” “framing,” and the topic map are interpretations of those indicators, not causal or technical conclusions.
